title: Valid Until Renewal: The Non-Domiciled CDL Rule, a Pending D.C. Circuit Ruling and the Driver File
summary: FMCSA's non-domiciled CDL rule is in force while the D.C. Circuit weighs it. What carriers, brokers and shippers should verify, document and decide now.
body_markdown:
A safety manager at a 60-truck dry van fleet pulls the driver roster in November and sorts it by license expiration. Four drivers hold non-domiciled CDLs. Two renew in December. Neither holds H-2A, H-2B or E-2 status. Both run dedicated lanes through the holidays. The decision in front of her is not abstract: build coverage now for two seats that may go empty at renewal, or wait for a federal appeals court that has had the case under submission since September.


The scenario is illustrative. The rule behind it is not. For U.S. carriers, brokers and shippers, the non-domiciled CDL rule is now a driver qualification question, a capacity question and, after the Supreme Court's broker decision in May, a liability documentation question at the same time.


## What the rule actually does


The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration published its interim final rule on Sept. 29, 2025. The D.C. Circuit stayed it in November 2025, but trade press reported that FMCSA had already placed many states under special instructions not to issue non-domiciled credentials, and those instructions were not covered by the court's stay.


FMCSA then published a final rule on Feb. 13, 2026 (91 FR 7044), effective March 16, 2026, which largely reaffirms the interim version. The key provisions, from the rule text:


-


Eligibility for a non-domiciled CDL or CLP is limited to drivers in H-2A, H-2B or E-2 employment-based nonimmigrant status.


-


Applicants show an unexpired foreign passport and a Form I-94 at issuance, transfer, renewal and upgrade. An Employment Authorization Document alone no longer qualifies.


-


The credential expires on the I-94 date or after one year, whichever is sooner.


-


Drivers must renew in person, and a state must downgrade the credential if it learns the holder is no longer eligible.


FMCSA estimated about 200,000 non-domiciled CDL holders and about 20,000 non-domiciled CLP holders. It expects roughly 6,000 non-domiciled CDLs a year to be issued to eligible drivers, and the remaining roughly 194,000 current holders to exit the freight market over about five years as credentials come up for renewal. The agency put the total at roughly 5% of the 3.8 million active interstate CDL holders in 2024. It also said it identified 17 fatal crashes in 2025 caused by non-domiciled CDL holders who would be ineligible under the new rule.


In a May 14, 2026 exemption decision, FMCSA allowed all state licensing agencies to issue non-domiciled credentials for five years to citizens of the Freely Associated States (Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau) who reside in the U.S. and hold a valid passport and I-94.


The practical point for operations: an existing non-domiciled CDL generally stays valid until it expires, so the rule bites at renewal or when a state cancels or downgrades a license early. That makes the expiration date column in your driver file the most important field in this story.


## Where the litigation stands


The challenge to the final rule is Lujan v. FMCSA, No. 26-1032, consolidated with No. 26-1046. Petitioners include two drivers and two labor unions.


On May 5, 2026, a D.C. Circuit motions panel denied a stay pending review by a 2-1 vote and expedited the case. A statement by Judge Katsas, joined by Judge Rao, said the petitioners had not met the stringent requirements for a stay. Judge Wilkins would have granted it. That order is why the rule is in force today.


The merits panel, Judges Millett, Pillard and Childs, heard argument on Sept. 15, 2026. Trade press coverage of the argument reported pointed questions to the government about whether the three permitted visa categories actually fit FMCSA's rationale that states cannot verify foreign driving histories, along with at least one judge appearing to credit that concern. Questions at argument do not predict outcomes. As of Nov. 10, trade coverage still described the rule as awaiting a decision.


The state fights run in parallel. On Jan. 7, 2026, the U.S. Department of Transportation said it was withholding $160 million in federal funds from California for failing to cancel more than 17,000 non-domiciled CDLs it considered improperly issued. California's challenge to that determination was argued in the D.C. Circuit on Sept. 11. New York brought a similar challenge over federal funds, set for argument on Sept. 28.


Even a loss for the agency would not automatically reopen issuance in states still under special instructions. Plan for the rule as written and treat a reversal as upside, not a scheduling assumption.


## Why this is now a broker liability question too


On May 14, 2026, in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, the Supreme Court held unanimously that the FAAAA does not preempt state negligent-hiring claims against freight brokers. Justice Barrett wrote that such claims fall within the safety exception in 49 U.S.C. 14501(c)(2)(A) because requiring a broker to use ordinary care in selecting a carrier concerns motor vehicles. The case had been argued March 4.


Justice Kavanaugh, joined by Justice Alito, concurred to stress that brokers should be able to defend these suits successfully "if the brokers have acted reasonably and arranged transportation with reputable trucking companies." He quoted plaintiff's counsel at argument: brokers "just have to hire carriers that actually have a reasonable policy," and "the broker is not going to have a problem if it's asking the hard questions of the carrier."


Put the two developments side by side. A federal rule is moving an estimated six-figure population of drivers toward license expiration over five years, and the agency itself has tied the policy to fatal crashes. A plaintiff's lawyer reconstructing a broker's selection decision after a serious crash will ask what the broker knew about the carrier's driver qualification practices, including how it handles licenses that are expiring, downgraded or cancelled. "We checked the authority and the insurance certificate" is a weaker answer in 2026 than it was in 2024.


None of this makes brokers responsible for checking individual drivers' immigration status, and they should not try. The defensible position is narrower: the broker asked the carrier the hard questions about its qualification process, recorded the answers, and acted on red flags.


## What asset carriers need to get right


The carrier is where federal duties sit. Carriers already must obtain a motor vehicle record from each state where a driver held a license at hire and review each driver's record at least once every 12 months (49 CFR 391.23 and 391.25). Under 49 CFR 383.37, an employer may not knowingly allow a driver to operate a CMV while the driver's CDL is suspended, revoked, cancelled or disqualified.


The non-domiciled rule changes the tempo of that work in three ways:


-


**Expiration windows are shorter.** A one-year maximum term means some drivers will renew every year, in person. Annual MVR cadence is no longer enough to catch a lapse.


-


**Downgrades can happen early.** A state that cancels or downgrades licenses under federal pressure can take a driver off the road with months left on the card. The record may show it before the driver tells you.


-


**Leased-on owner-operators count.** If a driver hauls under your authority, the qualification file is yours, whether the tractor is or not.


Capacity planning follows the same calendar. If two drivers on a dedicated account cannot renew in December, that is a customer conversation to have in November, not on the day the credential lapses. FMCSA's own estimate frames this as a five-year drawdown, which means a steady, predictable stream of renewals rather than one cliff.


## What brokers and shippers should ask


Brokers do not run carriers' driver files, but they decide which carriers get tendered. After Montgomery, the selection record should show reasonable inquiry, not just a status check:


-


At onboarding, ask the carrier to describe its process for monitoring license validity between annual reviews, and record the answer.


-


Treat recent out-of-service orders for driver qualification or licensing violations as a review trigger, not a footnote.


-


Define who can override a carrier review hold during peak, and require a reason when they do.


-


Keep the carrier packet, the review notes and the tender decision together, timestamped, for as long as your claims exposure runs.


Shippers that select carriers directly face the same negligent-selection theory in many states. Shippers that rely on brokers should know what their broker's selection policy actually says and whether contract indemnity and insurance obligations reflect it.


On contracts, read the carrier-broker agreement for a representation that drivers are properly licensed and qualified under Parts 383 and 391, a duty to notify of disqualifications on active loads, and an indemnity that survives termination. A broker's contingent auto liability coverage is a backstop, not a substitute for a selection process the broker can explain to a jury.


## The decisions to make this month


For carriers:


1.


Inventory every non-domiciled CDL in your files, including leased-on drivers, with the expiration date and the documented status basis.


2.


Move license monitoring for those drivers from annual to an interval tied to expiration.


3.


Build replacement coverage for any driver who cannot renew before the date, and tell affected customers early.


For brokers:


1.


Add driver qualification monitoring questions to carrier onboarding and recertification.


2.


Make the review outcome a status that blocks tendering until someone with authority clears it.


3.


Test whether you could produce the full selection record for a load from last March in under an hour.


For shippers:


1.


Ask brokers for their written carrier selection policy and how exceptions are approved.


2.


Align indemnity and insurance requirements with that policy.


## Encoding the rules


Every operation has its own mix of leased-on drivers, dedicated accounts and spot carriers, and its own appetite for exceptions during peak. That is why the defensible answer is rarely a single checklist. It is a set of rules your system enforces the same way every time: an expiration field that drives an alert sequence, a driver status that blocks dispatch when a credential lapses, a carrier status that blocks tendering until review is complete, permissions on who can override, and an audit trail that captures who decided what and why. When the D.C. Circuit rules, the shops that encoded their process will change a setting. The ones that did not will be rebuilding a file from email.


## FAQ


### Is the non-domiciled CDL rule in effect right now?


Yes, the final rule has been in effect since March 16, 2026, after the D.C. Circuit denied a stay on May 5, 2026. The merits panel heard argument on Sept. 15, 2026 and, as of Nov. 10, had not issued a decision.


### Do existing non-domiciled CDLs become invalid immediately?


No, an existing credential generally remains valid until it expires, unless a state cancels or downgrades it earlier. At renewal, the driver must meet the new eligibility and documentation requirements, including H-2A, H-2B or E-2 status and a passport with Form I-94.


### How many drivers could the rule affect?


FMCSA estimated about 200,000 non-domiciled CDL holders, of whom roughly 194,000 would exit the freight market over about five years as credentials come up for renewal. The agency expects about 6,000 non-domiciled CDLs a year to be issued to eligible drivers.


### Should brokers check drivers' immigration status?


No, brokers should not try to verify individual drivers' immigration status, which is the carrier's and the state's domain. After Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, the stronger position is documenting that you asked carriers how they monitor driver license validity and acted on red flags.


### What happens if the D.C. Circuit strikes the rule down?


The court could vacate the rule or send it back to FMCSA, but that would not automatically restart issuance in states operating under separate federal special instructions. Plan around the current rule and treat any reversal as added flexibility rather than a planning assumption.
